story_type: first ever flight of a moon rocket, uncrewed, onboard cameras film stage separation, capsule recovered at sea
hook: The first Saturn V ever flown. Nobody was aboard.
narration: The first Saturn V ever launched flew with nobody aboard.
On November ninth, 1967, its five engines lit beneath six million pounds of rocket.
Together they made seven and a half million pounds of thrust.
NASA flew every stage live on this very first flight, all at once, instead of testing them one at a time.
At thirty nine miles up, the first stage engines shut down.
Cameras on the rocket filmed the stages pulling apart.
In orbit, the spacecraft fired its own engine and climbed more than eleven thousand miles out.
Then it dove back in at over twenty five thousand miles per hour to test the heat shield.
outcome: Eight hours and thirty six minutes after liftoff, the capsule landed in the Pacific within sight of the carrier Bennington.
title: First Saturn V flew with nobody aboard
description:
On Nov. 9, 1967, Apollo 4 made the first flight of the Saturn V moon rocket with no crew aboard. Onboard cameras filmed first stage separation, and the capsule landed in the Pacific near the carrier Bennington after testing its heat shield.
